title: The Blacksmith Who Could Handle Fire

keywords: the blacksmith who could handle fire
full_text:
A traveler visiting the market of Basra stopped before a blacksmith’s forge, astounded by what his eyes beheld: the blacksmith was reaching with his bare hands into the roaring furnace, lifting red-hot iron bars from the coals, and hammering them upon the anvil without burning his skin or suffering the slightest pain!

When the work was finished, the traveler approached respectfully and asked: 'O master smith, by what miracle or counter-sorcery does your flesh remain unharmed by glowing coals?'

The blacksmith sighed and answered: 'It is neither sorcery nor magic, brother, but the fruit of an hour of supreme trial in my youth.

In my early years, a terrible famine struck our city. A young woman of peerless beauty and noble family, whom I had long admired in secret, came to my house at midnight, starving and begging for a loaf of bread for her dying children. In my youthful weakness, I was tempted to demand that she compromise her honor in exchange for food.

The noble maiden wept bitterly, saying: "Shall you exploit the hunger of the destitute? Remember that the fire of conscience burns hotter than the furnaces of earth!"

Her words pierced my heart like a sword. Shame struck my soul; I repented immediately, wept before her, and gave her all the flour and gold in my house freely, accompanying her safely to her children.

She lifted her hands to heaven and prayed: "May the Creator who protected my honor preserve your flesh from the fire in this world and the next!"

The next morning, when I accidentally touched a burning iron bar in my forge, I felt only the coolness of rose petals. Since that day, fire has no dominion over my hands, reminding me that overcoming temptation is the greatest armor a man can wear.'
moral: Self-restraint, protecting the vulnerable, and overcoming temptation grant divine protection.
